Fannie Barrier Williams, a longtime resident, was among those the club pressed to leave, and she refused.

facts.display: Buchanan v. Warley, 1917

source.title: Buchanan v. Warley, 245 U.S. 60
source.author: U.S. Supreme Court

facts.notes: Holding. City ordinances zoning blocks by race violate the Fourteenth Amendment. Consequence. With racial zoning off the table, segregationists shifted to private deed covenants, which the ordinance ruling did not touch.

facts.display: Corrigan v. Buckley, 1926

source.title: Corrigan v. Buckley, 271 U.S. 323
source.author: U.S. Supreme Court

secondarySources: Chicago Covenants Project history
facts.notes: Holding. The Court dismissed a constitutional challenge to a private racial covenant, holding the constitutional claims raised no substantial federal question against private agreements. Consequence. The industry treated covenants as court-proof and they proliferated through the late 1920s and 1930s.

facts.display: Hansberry v. Lee, 1940

source.title: Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32
source.author: U.S. Supreme Court

facts.notes: Holding. An earlier class judgment upholding the Washington Park covenant could not bind Carl Hansberry consistent with due process. Consequence. The family kept the house at 6140 South Rhodes, but the ruling left covenants themselves standing.

source.author: U.S. Supreme Court
source.locator: 6 to 0, Chief Justice Vinson writing, three justices recused

facts.notes: Holding. Judicial enforcement of racially restrictive covenants is state action barred by the Fourteenth Amendment. Consequence. The clauses became unenforceable but stayed printed in deeds, and Black families finally began crossing into Hyde Park and Kenwood.

facts.display: the federal Housing Act of 1949

source.title: Housing Act of 1949
source.author: United States Congress
source.locator: Public Law 81-171, 63 Stat. 413, Title I, July 15, 1949

facts.notes: Title I put federal money behind slum clearance and urban redevelopment. A city could declare an area blighted, condemn and clear the land, and resell it to private redevelopers below cost, with federal capital grants absorbing most of the write-down. Registered for the exhibit wall text; the Hyde Park program ran on this statute and its later amendments, with Section 112 (1959) supplying the university's lever.

facts.notes: King and Coretta Scott King moved into a flat at 1550 South Hamlin Avenue on January 26, 1966 to lead the Chicago Freedom Movement's housing campaign. The open housing marches of July and August 1966 into Gage Park and Marquette Park met organized violence; a thrown stone struck King on August 5, 1966, and a nonbinding summit agreement followed on August 26.
